cards.title: Talk to first customers and keep it in your culture
cards.summary: Regardless of business type, understand what you solve for customers and keep talking to buyers from day one instead of stopping after launch.
cards.use_when: Starting or scaling any business and deciding whether to institutionalize customer conversations.

cards.title: Cross-check what people say against what they do
cards.summary: Conversations reveal the why of behavior but people can misreport what they do; digital intelligence and listening data show actual behavior.
cards.use_when: Reconciling conflicting evidence between interviews and analytics/listening data, or designing research to minimize blind spots.

cards.title: Apply jobs-to-be-done using the milkshake story
cards.summary: The milkshake case is a compact way to explain JTBD to clients and teams before applying it to their business.
cards.use_when: Introducing jobs-to-be-done to a client or internal team that has not encountered it.

cards.title: Use the Value Equation to Diagnose a Product Offer
cards.summary: Increase a product offer’s perceived value by improving the desired outcome and confidence while reducing wait time and customer effort.
cards.use_when: Designing a product bundle, subscription, or product-page promise that shoppers currently compare mainly by price.

cards.title: Create a Category-of-One Product Bundle
cards.summary: Escape direct price comparison by packaging a distinct, credible outcome rather than selling an interchangeable item alone.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a commodity-like product category where shoppers can easily compare your SKU, price, and shipping terms with competitors.

cards.title: Build Product Bundles With Trim and Stack
cards.summary: Turn the obstacles customers face into a focused bundle of product components, guidance, and add-ons that are valuable to buyers and economical to fulfill.
cards.use_when: Creating kits, gift sets, starter bundles, or subscription tiers to raise average order value without adding low-value fulfillment complexity.

cards.title: Choose an Ecommerce-Appropriate Guarantee Structure
cards.summary: Select unconditional, conditional, or no-refund terms based on product controllability, return exposure, and the specific buyer risk you need to reduce.
cards.use_when: Writing return, satisfaction, fit, delivery, or product-support terms for a PDP, cart, or checkout where hesitation centers on wasting money.

cards.title: Evaluate Guarantee Economics With Net Contribution
cards.summary: A stronger guarantee is worthwhile only when incremental orders produce more contribution than refunds, returns, and associated fulfillment costs consume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add or expand a return, satisfaction, replacement, or make-good promise for an ecommerce product offer.

cards.title: Use Truthful Urgency for Product Launches and Promotions
cards.summary: Give shoppers a real reason to act now through dated launches, seasonal windows, expiring offer terms, or genuinely time-sensitive inventory opportunities.
cards.use_when: Planning a product drop, preorder, seasonal campaign, or time-bound bundle when customers tend to postpone a decision.

cards.title: Apply Honest Scarcity to Inventory and Bonuses
cards.summary: Use real limits on inventory, production capacity, or a defined bonus allocation to communicate availability without creating false pressure.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a limited product run, constrained seasonal inventory, made-to-order capacity, or first-buyer bonus during a launch.

cards.title: Name a Bundle So Shoppers Understand It Immediately
cards.summary: Use the M-A-G-I-C naming elements—Magnet, Avatar, Goal, Interval, and Container—to make a kit or promotion easier to understand and remember.
cards.use_when: Naming a product kit, collection, seasonal promotion, subscription tier, or replenishment program for a specific customer use case.

cards.title: Maintain Offer Congruence From Ad Through Post-Purchase
cards.summary: Keep price, contents, incentives, guarantee, and deadline consistent across every customer touchpoint so shoppers do not discover conflicting terms after clicking or buying.
cards.use_when: Launching or changing a promotion, bundle, bonus, guarantee, or pricing structure across paid acquisition, storefront, checkout, and lifecycle email.

cards.title: Use Anchors and Decoys to Guide Bundle Choice
cards.summary: Present a credible premium reference and well-structured tiers so the intended product bundle has a clearer value context without changing its actual price.
cards.use_when: Structuring a collection, bundle selector, subscription tier page, or product comparison table where shoppers struggle to choose among options.

cards.title: Design Bonuses That Remove Purchase Obstacles
cards.summary: Use relevant, economical bonuses to resolve a real barrier to using the main product instead of discounting its list price.
cards.use_when: Improving a product launch, bundle, or cart incentive when shoppers understand the main item but hesitate over setup, selection, compatibility, or missing accessories.

cards.title: Gate Offer Changes With Contribution Margin
cards.summary: Approve discounts, bundles, bonuses, guarantees, and shipping incentives only after evaluating their effect on net contribution, not conversion or revenue alone.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a proposed ecommerce offer change before it reaches paid traffic, email subscribers, or the storefront.

cards.title: Grand Slam Offer: make the product offer hard to compare
cards.summary: Package products, bonuses, guarantees, and payment terms so shoppers evaluate your store’s outcome and total value rather than a competitor’s unit price.
cards.use_when: Reworking a flagship product, kit, bundle, or subscription because shoppers can easily find an apparently identical item for less.

cards.title: The starving crowd: choose product demand before polishing the offer
cards.summary: Prioritize categories and customer problems with urgent, visible demand before spending heavily on product packaging, copy, or promotional mechanics.
cards.use_when: Choosing a new product category, customer segment, seasonal inventory buy, or product concept to launch in an online store.

cards.title: Use the three growth levers to prioritize store work
cards.summary: Organize ecommerce growth around acquiring more customers, increasing profit per purchase, and increasing purchase frequency per customer.
cards.use_when: Selecting whether the next store initiative should focus on acquisition, product and cart merchandising, pricing, bundles, retention, or replenishment.

cards.title: Calculate lifetime gross profit before setting acquisition and offer spend
cards.summary: Use gross profit per order and expected repeat purchases to estimate lifetime gross profit, then set product, promotion, and acquisition decisions against that figure.
cards.use_when: Setting CAC guardrails, evaluating paid-media scale, choosing bundle discounts, or deciding whether a subscription or replenishment offer can support its incentives.

cards.title: Fix price-driven shopping by differentiating the merchandise offer
cards.summary: When shoppers see your product as interchangeable, change the offer and product presentation so the decision rests on value, fit, and outcome rather than the lowest listed price.
cards.use_when: A product page, collection, or paid campaign is attracting price objections, competitor comparisons, frequent discount requests, or poor conversion despite competitive pricing.

cards.title: Market selection: screen a product niche on four indicators
cards.summary: Choose product markets with acute pain, sufficient buyer spending power, reachable audiences, and stable or growing demand.
cards.use_when: Selecting a new product category, launching a specialty storefront, or deciding whether to keep investing in an underperforming ecommerce niche.

cards.title: Diagnose growth in order: market, offer, then persuasion
cards.summary: Assess demand quality before rebuilding product pages or ads, then strengthen the offer before relying on exceptional copywriting.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a weak ecommerce launch needs a category change, a better bundle and proposition, or better acquisition creative.

cards.title: Use evergreen demand buckets to generate category ideas
cards.summary: Generate category candidates from health, wealth, and relationships, then validate a specific buyer subgroup rather than selling to everyone.
cards.use_when: Building a list of possible ecommerce categories or deciding how to narrow a broad product assortment.

cards.title: Commit to a product-market long enough to learn
cards.summary: Do not mistake a failed product launch or offer for a failed niche; keep the audience fixed long enough to iterate meaningfully.
cards.use_when: Considering abandoning a product category after disappointing conversion, paid-acquisition, or repeat-purchase results.

cards.title: Use specificity to support premium pricing
cards.summary: A more specific product for a buyer with a high-value use case can command more than a generic version of the same core solution.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product line, kit, subscription, or digital add-on for a narrowly defined shopper segment.

cards.title: Compete by enlarging value, not by copying low prices
cards.summary: Avoid automatic undercutting; improve the buyer’s value-to-price gap through a better product, bundle, experience, or proof.
cards.use_when: Setting prices against marketplace competitors or deciding whether to respond to a competitor’s discount with a lower storefront price.

cards.title: Use price as part of the product experience
cards.summary: For products requiring customer participation, a higher price can increase commitment and perceived value, but only if delivery supports the expectation.
cards.use_when: Considering a price increase for a product, kit, subscription, or replenishment program where buyer follow-through affects results.

cards.title: Build a category-of-one premium position
cards.summary: A price far above commodity alternatives can signal a categorically different offer when supported by tangible differentiation and proof.
cards.use_when: Launching a premium bundle, flagship product, or high-AOV collection into a crowded commodity category.

cards.title: Audit every offer with the value equation
cards.summary: Increase dream outcome and confidence while reducing perceived delay, effort, and sacrifice to make a product more valuable.
cards.use_when: Reworking a PDP, bundle, subscription proposition, or checkout offer that shoppers perceive as expensive or inconvenient.

cards.title: Make value improvements visible to the shopper
cards.summary: Operational improvements only improve conversion when customers can perceive and understand them at the buying moment.
cards.use_when: A store has better delivery, quality, product performance, or service than competitors but shoppers still compare it as a commodity.

cards.title: Frame the dream outcome in socially meaningful terms
cards.summary: Lead product messaging with the desired transformation and its social meaning rather than a disconnected feature list.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero section and benefit hierarchy for a product page, landing page, or acquisition creative.

cards.title: Raise perceived likelihood with credible proof
cards.summary: Make shoppers confident that the product will work for their use case through evidence, transparent details, and appropriate risk reversal.
cards.use_when: Choosing reviews, demonstrations, guarantees, comparison content, or product claims for a PDP or landing page.

cards.title: Deliver a fast, genuine first win after purchase
cards.summary: Use fulfillment, onboarding, and early product use to give customers a quick tangible or emotional win while the longer-term outcome develops.
cards.use_when: Designing unboxing, post-purchase email, first-use guidance, or a replenishment onboarding sequence for a product with delayed results.

cards.title: Remove customer effort from product use and replenishment
cards.summary: Increase value by reducing the waiting, learning, assembly, coordination, and risk that customers bear before receiving the benefit.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a physical product, bundle, subscription flow, or post-purchase experience that has low activation or repeat purchase.

cards.title: Price from buyer value while protecting fulfillment margin
cards.summary: Set price from the value and differentiation delivered, not merely manufacturing cost, while retaining margin to fulfill the promise well.
cards.use_when: Establishing list price and margin requirements for a new SKU, premium bundle, or subscription offer.

cards.title: Repackage around the product element customers value most
cards.summary: Use customer purchase and review evidence to concentrate a product or bundle on its highest-value job instead of adding generic extras.
cards.use_when: Simplifying an existing assortment, rebuilding a bundle, or preparing a price increase for a product with too many low-value inclusions.

cards.title: Treat price increases as an operational decision, not a coupon substitute
cards.summary: Raise prices only alongside a stronger customer experience and measurement plan; do not use discounting as the default response to stalled growth.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase list price, end persistent promotions, or reduce coupon dependence on an ecommerce storefront.

cards.title: Recognize when the category—not the offer—is the constraint
cards.summary: If demand is structurally shrinking, a strong product and well-executed offer may still be the wrong place to invest.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to continue optimizing an ecommerce category after repeated offer, product-page, and acquisition tests fail to produce sustainable growth.

cards.title: Engineer fast wins into long-timeline product outcomes
cards.summary: Give customers an early, noticeable benefit that reinforces their purchase decision before the headline result can realistically arrive.
cards.use_when: Designing post-purchase onboarding, replenishment, or subscription retention for products with slow outcomes, such as skincare, supplements, fitness equipment, or multi-step routines.

cards.title: Compete against free by selling speed
cards.summary: When buyers can use a free alternative, position the paid product around getting the desired result faster and with less waiting.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product or digital download against DIY methods, free content, generic tools, or slow low-cost alternatives.

cards.title: Diagnose offer value with four buyer drivers
cards.summary: Compare offers by the desired outcome, perceived likelihood, time to result, and required effort, then improve the weakest driver.
cards.use_when: Choosing between product formats, bundles, price points, or PDP messages for items that solve the same customer problem in different ways.

cards.title: Reduce customer effort and sacrifice in the product offer
cards.summary: Make the same desired outcome more valuable by removing setup, learning, coordination, and other hidden costs the customer bears.
cards.use_when: Customers hesitate at checkout, fail to use a product correctly, or churn from replenishment because the solution feels difficult or inconvenient.

cards.title: Generate non-obvious bundle and product-format ideas
cards.summary: Use divergent thinking to create many ways an existing product asset can solve a customer desire before selecting the viable options.
cards.use_when: Planning bundles, variants, digital add-ons, packaging formats, or merchandising angles when the catalog resembles competitors' offerings.

cards.title: Sell the destination rather than the commodity SKU
cards.summary: Position a product or bundle as a credible path to a desired end state so buyers compare it with the outcome, not a cheaper interchangeable item.
cards.use_when: A PDP or landing page is losing to low-cost commodity comparisons, such as a generic subscription, single SKU, or inexpensive alternative.

cards.title: Map the full customer obstacle sequence before building a bundle
cards.summary: List every obstacle customers encounter before, during, and after using a product so the offer solves the sequence rather than one isolated problem.
cards.use_when: Rebuilding a product bundle, landing page, onboarding sequence, or retention flow after discovering recurring hesitation and product-use failures.

cards.title: Turn customer obstacles into concrete offer components
cards.summary: Reverse each meaningful buyer problem into a deliverable, instruction, or product feature that can be included and clearly explained in the offer.
cards.use_when: Turning customer research into a bundle specification, PDP content plan, packaging insert, bonus, or post-purchase support asset.

cards.title: Design scalable delivery formats for each product solution
cards.summary: Choose whether each customer solution should be embedded in the product, delivered as self-service content, or reserved for higher-priced support.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to fulfill bundle benefits, product education, personalization, and support without creating an unscalable manual workload.

cards.title: Trim offer components by customer value and fulfillment cost
cards.summary: Keep benefits that strongly improve the buyer's outcome, confidence, speed, or ease while removing low-value complexity and protecting margin.
cards.use_when: Selecting which bundle components, bonuses, content assets, and support promises belong in a product offer.

cards.title: Convert recurring objections into reusable ecommerce assets
cards.summary: When one objection repeatedly stops purchases or correct use, create a standard product, content, or policy solution instead of repeatedly arguing with customers.
cards.use_when: Support conversations, reviews, returns, or abandonment research reveal the same late-stage objection on a PDP or at checkout.

cards.title: Assemble a named, outcome-oriented bundle
cards.summary: Package retained solutions into a coherent kit with clear names, tangible benefits, and a price that is understood against the complete outcome path.
cards.use_when: Launching a starter kit, gift set, routine bundle, subscription box, or premium product package.

cards.title: Start with high-service validation, then systematize fulfillment
cards.summary: Use early demand and customer feedback to learn what support matters, then replace expensive manual fulfillment with scalable systems that preserve the core outcome.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product bundle, premium subscription, or complex onboarding experience before its repeatable operations are fully proven.

cards.title: Use real scarcity for limited drops and constrained inventory
cards.summary: When supply is genuinely limited, make the constraint clear and use it to focus demand, protect operations, and support a premium price.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a limited-edition product, numbered release, seasonal inventory, made-to-order run, or capacity-constrained premium bundle.

cards.title: Capture reviews with a specific, low-friction post-purchase ask
cards.summary: Ask satisfied customers for one simple review action at the moment of highest product satisfaction, with current platform-specific instructions.
cards.use_when: Building product-page social proof, improving marketplace review volume, or creating a referral and review flow after delivery or successful first use.

cards.title: Keep Product Supply Below Demand for Compounding Drop Demand
cards.summary: For limited ecommerce releases, consistently selling out a genuinely capped run can build pent-up demand for the next drop.
cards.use_when: Planning inventory depth, unit caps, and release cadence for limited-edition products, seasonal variants, collectibles, or special bundles.

cards.title: Build Premium Product Price Power Through Specialized Outcomes
cards.summary: A premium product earns pricing power when it solves a highly specific, valuable problem that customers perceive few alternatives can solve.
cards.use_when: Positioning a premium SKU, kit, bundle, customization option, or flagship collection against cheaper commodity alternatives.

cards.title: Use Genuine Time Deadlines to Turn Product Interest Into Decisions
cards.summary: Quantity scarcity and time urgency are separate levers; a real purchase cutoff can prompt action without changing the underlying product.
cards.use_when: Setting a deadline for a limited product drop, seasonal bundle, gift-with-purchase, preorder window, or temporary promotional price.

cards.title: Refresh Seasonal Promotion Wrappers Without Pretending the Offer Disappears
cards.summary: A dated seasonal wrapper can make a familiar product promotion feel timely, provided the published date and changing promotional element are real.
cards.use_when: Building a yearly calendar for ecommerce promotions, especially when the core catalog remains available year-round.

cards.title: Use Bonus Stacks Instead of Automatically Discounting the Core Product
cards.summary: Present a product offer as a core purchase plus named, relevant additions to increase perceived value without teaching shoppers to wait for price cuts.
cards.use_when: Structuring a PDP, bundle landing page, cart offer, or launch promotion where price resistance is high but margin makes discounting undesirable.

cards.title: Design Ecommerce Bonuses That Answer Purchase Objections
cards.summary: The strongest product bonuses are named, easy-to-use assets or extras that solve a specific buying objection and make the core purchase easier to succeed with.
cards.use_when: Choosing bonuses for a product launch, bundle, subscription acquisition offer, or cart conversion campaign.

cards.title: Build a Reusable Bonus Vault and Adjacent-Brand Partner Offers
cards.summary: Create low-marginal-cost customer tools and partner perks that solve the next need created by your product, then use them in bundles and retention campaigns.
cards.use_when: Building a repeatable source of launch bonuses, post-purchase resources, and cross-brand offers for an ecommerce customer base.

cards.title: Model Guarantee Economics Before Strengthening Refund Terms
cards.summary: A stronger guarantee can still improve net sales even if refund rate rises, so evaluate the incremental sales and refunds rather than reacting to refund risk alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to offer a longer return window, satisfaction guarantee, trial period, or outcome-linked guarantee for an ecommerce product.

cards.title: Choose an Ecommerce Guarantee Structure That Fits Product Economics
cards.summary: Match unconditional, conditional, anti-, or implied guarantees to the product’s returnability, customer risk, and cost of fulfillment.
cards.use_when: Writing return, refund, performance, subscription, or satisfaction terms for a new product, premium bundle, or replenishment offer.

cards.title: Stack Guarantees Only When Each Layer Removes a Different Ecommerce Risk
cards.summary: Multiple compatible guarantees can reduce different buying fears, but the merchant must model the combined worst-case cost and honor every layer.
cards.use_when: Designing risk reversal for a premium physical product, complex kit, subscription starter offer, or high-consideration bundle.

cards.title: Write a Clear, Credible Satisfaction Guarantee for Lower-Ticket Products
cards.summary: A strong satisfaction guarantee postpones the buyer’s final judgment until after use, while giving a simple, truthful path to a refund or remedy.
cards.use_when: Writing the guarantee section for a lower-ticket consumer product page, bundle landing page, checkout, or launch email.

cards.title: Name Guarantees for Clarity and Brand Fit, Not Boilerplate
cards.summary: A vivid, benefit-led guarantee name makes a risk-reversal promise more noticeable than generic satisfaction language, provided the tone and remedy remain credible.
cards.use_when: Finalizing guarantee language for product pages, checkout reassurance, paid creative, or a launch landing page.

cards.title: Design product guarantees by reversing shopper risk
cards.summary: Build an ecommerce guarantee from the specific failure, hassle, and out-of-pocket cost shoppers fear when buying your product.
cards.use_when: Creating or revising a PDP, bundle landing page, or checkout guarantee for products where hesitation centers on fit, performance, delivery, or wasted spend.

cards.title: Use a finite first-outcome promise for activation
cards.summary: Tie a conditional benefit or later charge to a fast, repeatable first customer outcome so the offer drives product adoption rather than only initial purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing a starter kit, subscription trial, replenishment flow, or post-purchase onboarding for a product whose early use predicts repeat purchase.

cards.title: Use all-sales-final policies only for genuinely non-returnable value
cards.summary: An anti-guarantee can position a product as exclusive or immediately consumed, but only when a truthful reason makes returns impractical.
cards.use_when: Setting return policy and PDP messaging for digital products, personalized goods, made-to-order items, or products whose value cannot be returned once accessed.

cards.title: Name offers with the M-A-G-I-C formula
cards.summary: Create punchy promotion, bundle, and launch names by combining a magnet, avatar, goal, interval, and container, then test alternatives.
cards.use_when: Naming a seasonal promotion, starter bundle, product launch, subscription acquisition offer, or landing-page campaign.

cards.title: Name bundle components to raise perceived value
cards.summary: Apply offer naming to every bundle item so shoppers understand each component as a purposeful solution rather than a commodity line item.
cards.use_when: Building a value stack for a product bundle, gift set, subscription welcome box, cart upsell, or promotional landing page.

cards.title: Refresh offer fatigue from creative to economics
cards.summary: When campaign response declines, vary the least disruptive layer first—creative, copy, and offer wrapper—before changing the product bundle, discount, or price architecture.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing declining ad or landing-page performance for an established ecommerce promotion without creating unnecessary merchandising and operational complexity.

cards.title: Adapt offer rotation for local and geographically limited ecommerce
cards.summary: Use local relevance to strengthen trust, while planning more frequent creative and headline variation when a campaign repeatedly reaches a small geographic audience.
cards.use_when: Running ecommerce acquisition for a local retailer, delivery-radius brand, regional product launch, or store that uses local inventory and fulfillment as part of its proposition.

cards.title: Audit an ecommerce offer before scaling traffic
cards.summary: Before buying more traffic, verify that the product offer is differentiated, economically viable, clearly valued, and supported by scarcity, urgency, bonuses, risk reversal, and a resonant name where appropriate.
cards.use_when: Preparing a new product launch, bundle, promotional landing page, or acquisition campaign for additional paid traffic.

cards.title: Map the Value Equation onto a physical product
cards.summary: Adapt Hormozi's four value drivers — dream outcome, perceived likelihood, time delay, and effort/sacrifice — to DTC by finding the specific ecommerce lever for each variable.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a physical product converts worse than a comparable competitor, or planning which offer elements to add first.

cards.title: Layer guarantees instead of relying on a money-back policy
cards.summary: Treat a standard refund policy as table stakes and add a second, implied guarantee layer such as delayed-capture Try-Before-You-Buy billing to further lower purchase risk.
cards.use_when: A store already offers returns and wants an additional risk-reversal mechanism that moves the conversion needle.

cards.title: Use stock counts and time windows as separate scarcity levers
cards.summary: Scarcity (limited quantity) and urgency (limited time) are distinct ratchets — Amazon applies both, and drop models combine them.
cards.use_when: Planning launch mechanics, limited-edition releases, or a promo calendar for a DTC store.

cards.title: Stack zero-COGS digital bonuses on physical products
cards.summary: Attach informational assets — styling guides, usage protocols, pairing or combination guides — that raise perceived value without adding unit cost.
cards.use_when: Looking for ways to increase perceived value or AOV on a physical product without touching manufacturing cost or price.

cards.title: Name products after the outcome and the search phrase
cards.summary: Outcome-explicit naming signals the dream outcome and matches how buyers search, while generic names like 'jacket' leave the value implicit.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising product titles on a PDP, marketplace listing, or ad creative for a physical product.

cards.title: Out-offer competitors with the same underlying product
cards.summary: Two stores can sell identical goods and convert differently purely because one has checked the value variables and enhancers the other has not.
cards.use_when: Building an offer differentiation plan when the product itself is not unique, or auditing why a competitor wins on a comparable item.

cards.title: Apply the value equation to purchase conversion, not lead conversion
cards.summary: The Value Equation is presented as the general mechanism behind purchasing decisions — value must be perceived in excess of price — and is argued to apply to physical products as well as services.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to translate a services-origin framework (Hormozi's $100M Offers) into a DTC or physical-product business.
